When deciding between platforms, a **[TradingView](https://in.tradingview.com/?aff_id=167054) vs Thinkorswim comparison** helps traders see which tool fits their style, budget, and technical needs. Both are popular among retail investors, but they serve slightly different audiences. TradingView shines with its web‑based charts, social community, and extensive library of user‑generated indicators. Thinkorswim, offered by TD Ameritrade, provides a powerful desktop platform geared toward active traders who want advanced order types, paper trading, and deep integration with a brokerage account. Below we break down the most important aspects so you can choose the right fit.

## Key Features
### Real‑Time Data
TradingView offers real‑time data for many exchanges through its paid plans, while free users get delayed data for most U.S. stocks. Thinkorswim provides real‑time quotes and level II data at no extra cost for funded accounts, making it attractive for day traders who need up‑to‑the‑second pricing.

### Custom Indicators
Both platforms allow custom studies, but TradingView’s Pine Script language is known for its simplicity and large public script library. Thinkorsmim uses thinkScript, which is more complex but offers deeper access to order‑flow analytics and advanced studies built into the platform.

### Alerts System
TradingView lets you set alerts based on price, indicator crosses, or even webhook notifications that can trigger external services. Thinkorswim’s alert system is robust, supporting conditional orders, email/SMS alerts, and even audio cues directly within the desktop client.

## Charting Tools
### Drawing Tools
TradingView provides a wide array of drawing tools—trendlines, Fibonacci retracements, pitchforks, and shape annotations—all accessible via a clean toolbar. Thinkorswim matches this with a comparable set, plus additional tools like market profile and time‑sales overlays that cater to professional traders.
